modules.title: The Territory of Game Design
modules.overview: What is game design, and where does it begin and end? This module maps the full territory of the discipline — its history, its relationship to adjacent fields like game development and game studies, and the enormous variety of forms games take. You will examine how game designers think, what questions drive their practice, and why game design matters as a creative and cultural force. By the end, you will have a clear sense of the field you are entering and the scope of what you will learn.
objectives: Define game design and distinguish it from game development, game studies, and related fields
Describe the historical evolution of game design from folk games and board games to contemporary digital experiences
Identify the major roles and responsibilities of a game designer across different contexts
Articulate why game design is a significant creative, cultural, and professional discipline

resources.label: Game Design & Development 2021 — selected introductory chapters
MIT OpenCourseWare — 1-1: Introduction, Overview, and Syllabus for Game Design
Twine — browser editor for interactive, nonlinear stories

modules.reflectionPrompt: Think about a game that first made you want to design games. What was it about that game's design — its rules, its world, its feel — that sparked your interest? How does that experience connect to what you learned about the territory of game design today?

modules.title: Games, Rules, and Players
modules.overview: Every game is defined by its rules — the formal structures that tell players what they can do, what they cannot do, and what winning or losing means. This module examines the foundational relationship between games, their rule systems, and the players who engage with them. You will learn to distinguish between different types of rules, analyze how rules create possibility spaces, and understand how players interpret, negotiate, and sometimes subvert the rules they are given. Formal game analysis tools are introduced and applied to real examples.
objectives: Distinguish between constitutive rules, operational rules, and implicit rules in games
Explain how rules define a game's possibility space and constrain player behavior
Analyze how players interpret, negotiate, and subvert rules in practice
Apply formal game analysis to break down the rule structure of an existing game

resources.label: Game Design Concepts, Level 3: Formal Elements of Games
The Magic Circle
Twine

modules.reflectionPrompt: Pick a game you know well and identify one implicit rule — something players follow that is never written down. Where did that rule come from? What would happen to the game if it were made explicit, or if it were removed entirely?

modules.title: Play Communities
modules.overview: Games are not played in a vacuum — they exist within communities of players who share norms, histories, and social practices. This module explores how play communities form around games, how they evolve over time, and how they shape the meaning and reception of the games they play. You will examine competitive scenes, fan communities, modding cultures, and the social dynamics of multiplayer design. Crucially, you will also consider the designer's responsibility toward the communities their games create and sustain.
objectives: Describe how play communities form, sustain themselves, and evolve around games
Analyze the social norms, shared practices, and power dynamics within different play communities
Identify design decisions that shape the kind of community a game fosters
Reflect on the designer's ethical responsibilities toward the communities their games create

resources.label: Community codes of conduct as proactive intervention for toxicity in games
Games as Community Driven Care: A Case Study of Co-Designing Games for Health
itch.io Hosting a game jam (free community/jam workflow)

modules.reflectionPrompt: Describe a play community you have been part of — online or in person. What norms governed how people behaved? Were those norms healthy or harmful? What design decisions in the game itself encouraged or discouraged those norms?

modules.title: Building Blocks of Game Design
modules.overview: All games are built from the same fundamental elements — but the way those elements are combined is what makes each game unique. This module introduces the core building blocks of game design: mechanics, dynamics, aesthetics, components, resources, and feedback loops. Using the MDA (Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics) framework as a primary lens, you will deconstruct existing games and learn to see how individual design decisions cascade into full player experiences. This vocabulary will serve as your foundation for everything that follows.
objectives: Define and apply the MDA (Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics) framework to analyze games
Identify the core mechanics, feedback loops, and resource systems in a variety of games
Explain how dynamics emerge from the interaction of mechanics and player behavior
Use precise design vocabulary when discussing, analyzing, and critiquing games
topics: Verbs and Nouns of Game Design

resources.label: MIT OpenCourseWare: Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics — The MDA Framework (lesson transcript/audio)
MIT OpenCourseWare: 4. Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics — The MDA Framework (official lecture video)
GDevelop — free/open-source game editor for mechanics and feedback-loop prototyping

modules.reflectionPrompt: Choose a game you played recently and apply the MDA framework to it. What are its core mechanics? What dynamics emerge from those mechanics? What aesthetic experience do those dynamics produce? Did the designer achieve what you think they intended?

modules.title: Modes of Interaction
modules.overview: How players interact with a game — and with each other through a game — is one of the most consequential design decisions a designer makes. This module surveys the primary modes of player interaction: solo, cooperative, competitive, asymmetric, and hybrid structures. You will examine how each mode creates different social dynamics, emotional experiences, and design challenges. Through analysis and hands-on exercises, you will practice identifying and intentionally designing for specific interaction structures.
objectives: Identify and distinguish the primary modes of player interaction: solo, cooperative, competitive, and asymmetric
Analyze how interaction structures create different social dynamics and emotional experiences
Evaluate the design trade-offs between cooperative, competitive, and hybrid interaction models
Design a simple mechanic that leverages a specific interaction mode intentionally

resources.label: Exploring the Effects of Different Asymmetric Game Designs on User Experience in Collaborative Virtual Reality
The Sweet Spot of Asymmetric Design — BAFTA Games Live / Creative Assembly
PlayingCards.io Standard Deck / Custom Room

modules.reflectionPrompt: Think of a game that uses an interaction mode you find particularly compelling. Why does that mode work so well for that game? Now imagine the same game redesigned with a different interaction mode — what would change, and what would be lost?

modules.title: Emergent Behavior
modules.overview: Some of the most memorable moments in games are not scripted — they arise unexpectedly from the interaction of simple rules and player choices. This is emergence: complex, unpredictable, and often delightful behavior that no single rule produces on its own. This module explores how emergence works in game systems, why it is a hallmark of deep and replayable design, and how to create rule sets that invite it. You will study classic examples of emergence across tabletop and digital games, then prototype a simple rule set in Tabletopia to observe emergent behavior firsthand.
objectives: Define emergent behavior and explain why it is a valuable property in game design
Identify design conditions — rule simplicity, player freedom, system interaction — that promote emergence
Analyze case studies of emergence in well-known tabletop and digital games
Prototype a simple rule set in Tabletopia and document the emergent behaviors that arise during play

resources.label: Examining Emergent Gameplay — Game Developer
Emergence, Dynamic Narrative and Systems in Game Design — The Game Overanalyser
Particle Life — Sandbox Science

modules.reflectionPrompt: Describe a moment of emergence you have experienced in a game — a situation the designers almost certainly did not script but that arose naturally from the rules. What conditions in the game made that moment possible? How would you design a rule set to encourage more moments like it?

modules.title: Choice and Chance
modules.overview: Meaningful decisions and elements of chance are two of the most powerful tools in a game designer's toolkit. This module examines how choice and randomness function in games — how to design decisions that feel genuinely meaningful, how to use chance to create tension and variety, and how to balance the two so that players feel both in control and surprised. You will analyze dice mechanics, card draws, probability curves, and branching decision trees, and practice designing choice architectures for tabletop game prototypes.
objectives: Distinguish between meaningful choice and illusory choice in game design
Explain how randomness functions as a design tool for tension, variety, and fairness
Analyze probability distributions and their effect on player experience and game balance
Design a choice architecture or chance mechanism for a tabletop game prototype

resources.label: Meaningful Choice in Games: Practical Guide & Case Studies
James Ernest: Probability for Game Designers (Lecture)
McDie — Visual Probability Analysis Tool for Board Game Designers

modules.reflectionPrompt: Think of a game where you felt a decision was truly meaningful — where your choice genuinely mattered. Now think of a game where a decision felt like an illusion. What made the difference? How would you apply that insight to a mechanic you are designing?

modules.title: Ideation and Concepts
modules.overview: Every great game begins with a generative creative process. This module introduces a toolkit of ideation methodologies used by professional game designers: structured brainstorming, SCAMPER, constraint-based design, concept mapping, and reference gathering. You will practice generating large quantities of ideas, filtering them using design criteria, and developing the most promising concepts into clear, communicable design briefs. You will also learn how constraints — of time, materials, or theme — can serve as powerful creative catalysts rather than limitations.
objectives: Apply structured ideation methodologies including SCAMPER, mind mapping, and constraint-based design
Generate and evaluate game concepts using design criteria such as novelty, feasibility, and player appeal
Write a concise, compelling design brief or concept statement for an original game idea
Identify how creative constraints can accelerate and sharpen the ideation process

resources.label: Purdue Extension / 4-H — SCAMPER Part 1
Game Maker’s Toolkit — How to find amazing game ideas
WiseMapping — free online mind-map editor

modules.reflectionPrompt: Using the SCAMPER method, take a game you know well and generate at least three new concept variations by substituting, combining, or reversing one of its core elements. Which variation excites you most, and why? What design brief would you write for it?

modules.title: Fundamentals of Prototyping
modules.overview: A prototype is a designer's most important thinking tool — a physical or digital artifact that makes ideas testable. This module covers the principles and practices of low-fidelity prototyping for tabletop games: when to prototype, what to prototype, and how to build prototypes that answer specific design questions quickly and cheaply. You will create paper prototypes, card-based prototypes, and tile-based prototypes, learning to iterate rapidly without over-investing in any single version. The goal is not a finished game — it is a question answered.
objectives: Explain the purpose and value of low-fidelity prototyping in the design process
Identify the specific design question each prototype is built to answer
Construct a paper, card, or tile-based prototype for a simple game concept
Evaluate a prototype's effectiveness at answering its intended design question

resources.label: MIT ICE Lab — Unit 5 Activity 2: Low-Fidelity Prototyping
MIT OpenCourseWare — Project 1, Low Fidelity Prototyping
PlayingCards.io — Blank/custom virtual tabletop room

modules.reflectionPrompt: Build a paper prototype of a single mechanic from a game concept you have been thinking about. What design question did you set out to answer? What did the prototype reveal that you could not have discovered just by thinking about it?

modules.title: Playtesting and Iteration
modules.overview: Playtesting is the engine of game design improvement. Without it, a designer is guessing. This module teaches you how to design and run effective playtests, observe player behavior without interfering, collect meaningful feedback, and translate that feedback into specific design changes. You will learn the difference between internal and external playtesting, how to write a playtest protocol, and how to manage the emotional challenge of watching your design fail — and using that failure productively to drive the next iteration.
objectives: Design a structured playtest session with clear objectives and observation protocols
Distinguish between internal and external playtesting and know when to use each
Collect and analyze qualitative and quantitative playtest feedback without biasing results
Translate playtest findings into specific, prioritized design changes for the next iteration

resources.label: Level Design Book: Playtesting
The ULTIMATE Playtest Guide
itch.io Limited Playtests & Releases

modules.reflectionPrompt: After your most recent playtest session, what was the single most surprising thing you observed? Did players use a mechanic in a way you did not anticipate? How did that observation change your next design decision?

modules.title: Usability
modules.overview: A game that is hard to understand is a game that does not get played. This module applies usability principles from human-computer interaction and UX design to game design, focusing on how to make games learnable, legible, and enjoyable from the very first moment of play. You will study cognitive load, onboarding design, visual clarity, and rule communication — and learn to evaluate games for usability through structured observation and heuristic analysis. The goal is to remove friction between the player and the experience you want them to have.
objectives: Apply core usability heuristics to the design of game rules, components, and interfaces
Identify and diagnose common usability failures in tabletop and digital games
Design an onboarding experience that reduces cognitive load and supports new player learning
Evaluate a game's usability through structured observation and heuristic analysis

resources.label: 10 Usability Heuristics Applied to Video Games
The Gamer's Brain, Part 2: UX of Onboarding and Player Engagement
Useberry Free Plan — student usability study tool

modules.reflectionPrompt: Think about a game that taught you how to play without a tutorial — where the design itself guided you. What specific design choices made that possible? Now think about a game where the onboarding failed you. What would you change?

modules.title: Cultural Responsibility
modules.overview: Games reflect and reinforce cultural values — and game designers bear responsibility for the messages their games send. This module examines how games represent culture, identity, and power, and how designers can approach their work with greater cultural awareness and accountability. You will analyze case studies of games that have caused harm through cultural insensitivity or stereotyping, explore frameworks for conducting culturally informed research, and develop strategies for designing games that are respectful, accurate, and genuinely inclusive of the cultures they engage with.
objectives: Identify how games represent and reinforce cultural narratives, identities, and power structures
Analyze case studies of cultural misrepresentation or harm in published games
Apply a cultural responsibility framework to evaluate a design in progress
Develop strategies for conducting culturally informed research during the design process

resources.label: Playing For Keeps: Digital Games to Preserve Indigenous Languages & Traditions
Indigenous Culture in Video Games — Phoebe Watson
International Indigenous Design Charter: Protocols for Sharing Indigenous Knowledge in Professional Design Practice

modules.reflectionPrompt: Identify a game that engages with a culture other than the designer's own. How well does it represent that culture? What research or consultation would have improved it? If you were designing a game that engaged with a culture you are not part of, what steps would you take?

modules.title: Inclusivity and Accessibility
modules.overview: Inclusive game design means creating games that can be played and enjoyed by the widest possible range of people — regardless of ability, age, background, or identity. This module covers accessibility standards for digital games, inclusive design principles, and practical techniques for accommodating players with visual, auditory, motor, and cognitive differences. You will study the Game Accessibility Guidelines, examine how leading studios have implemented accessibility features, and conduct an accessibility audit of an existing game to propose concrete, implementable improvements.
objectives: Define inclusive design and accessibility in the context of digital and tabletop game design
Identify the major categories of accessibility barriers across visual, auditory, motor, and cognitive dimensions
Apply the Game Accessibility Guidelines to evaluate and improve a game design
Conduct an accessibility audit of an existing game and propose actionable design improvements

resources.label: Xbox Accessibility Guidelines V3.2 — Microsoft Game Development
Accessible Player Experiences (APX) — AbleGamers / Accessible Games
Gaming Accessibility Fundamentals Learning Path — Microsoft Learn

modules.reflectionPrompt: Choose a game you know well and conduct a quick accessibility audit using the Game Accessibility Guidelines. Which category of accessibility — visual, auditory, motor, or cognitive — is most neglected? What is one concrete change that would make the biggest difference for the most players?

modules.title: Digital Prototyping in Teams
modules.overview: Digital game prototyping is rarely a solo endeavor. This module focuses on the collaborative practices, tools, and workflows that enable small teams to build digital prototypes efficiently using a game engine. You will explore version control for game projects, asset pipelines, task management, and communication strategies for distributed teams. Through a hands-on sprint, you will contribute to a shared digital prototype — practicing the coordination and communication skills that professional game development demands.
objectives: Describe the roles and responsibilities within a small digital game development team
Use version control (Git) to manage a shared game project and resolve conflicts
Apply agile task management practices to plan and execute a digital prototyping sprint
Build a simple interactive prototype collaboratively using a game engine

resources.label: Godot Engine documentation — Version control systems
GitHub Docs — About repositories
QuickStart to Git version control for Godot 4.2

modules.reflectionPrompt: Reflect on a collaborative project you have worked on — in games or any other field. What was the biggest communication or coordination challenge? How did it affect the outcome? What workflow or tool would have helped most, and why?

modules.title: Development Practices
modules.overview: Professional game development follows established practices that keep projects on track, teams aligned, and quality high. This module introduces industry-standard development practices including pre-production planning, milestone-based scheduling, game design documentation, and quality assurance. You will learn how to write a game design document (GDD) that communicates your vision clearly, how to scope a project realistically for your resources, and how to manage the critical transition from prototype to production without losing the design's core intent.
objectives: Describe the stages of a professional game development pipeline from concept to release
Write a concise game design document (GDD) that communicates a design vision clearly to a team
Apply milestone-based planning to a game project of defined scope and resources
Identify common development pitfalls — scope creep, feature drift, poor documentation — and strategies for avoiding them

resources.label: How To: Write a Game Design Document — Game Developer
The Art of Pre-Production — GDC Festival of Gaming
GitHub Issues & Projects — official planning and tracking documentation

modules.reflectionPrompt: Write a one-page GDD for a game concept you have been developing. What was hardest to articulate clearly — the mechanics, the tone, the target audience, or the core loop? What does that difficulty tell you about where your design still needs more thinking?

modules.title: Game Feel
modules.overview: Game feel — sometimes called 'juice' — is the tactile, moment-to-moment sensation of interacting with a well-crafted game. It is what makes a jump feel satisfying, a hit feel impactful, or a menu feel responsive. This module explores the principles behind game feel: input responsiveness, animation feedback, sound design, screen shake, particle effects, and the subtle tuning that separates a polished game from a rough prototype. You will implement game feel improvements in a game engine and evaluate the difference they make to the player experience.
objectives: Define game feel and articulate its role in player satisfaction and engagement
Identify the key components of game feel: input latency, visual feedback, animation, and audio
Implement basic game feel improvements — screen shake, particles, sound — in a game engine prototype
Evaluate the game feel of an existing game using a structured rubric
topics: Visual Feedback: Screen Shake and Particles

resources.label: Designing Game Feel. A Survey — Martin Pichlmair and Mads Johansen
Juice it or lose it — Martin Jonasson and Petri Purho
Godot Engine documentation: Controllers, gamepads, and joysticks

modules.reflectionPrompt: Play a game for 10 minutes with your full attention on game feel rather than strategy. What specific moment felt the most satisfying? Break it down: what combination of input response, animation, sound, and visual feedback created that feeling? How would you recreate it?

modules.title: Project Scoping
modules.overview: One of the most common — and most preventable — causes of unfinished games is scope creep: the gradual expansion of a project beyond what a team can realistically deliver. This module teaches you how to scope a game project appropriately for your resources, timeline, and team size. You will practice identifying the minimum viable version of a game, cutting features without killing the design's core vision, and communicating scope decisions clearly to teammates and stakeholders. Realistic scoping is not a creative compromise — it is what makes shipping possible.
objectives: Define project scope and explain why scope management is critical in game development
Apply the 'core loop first' principle to identify the minimum viable version of a game
Use prioritization frameworks (MoSCoW, design pillars) to decide which features to cut, defer, or keep
Communicate scope decisions clearly in a project brief or design document

resources.label: Unity Learn — Create your production plan
Extra Credits — Making Your First Game: Minimum Viable Product — Scope Small, Start Right
GitHub Projects — About Projects

modules.reflectionPrompt: Take a game concept you are working on and list every feature you want it to have. Now cut the list in half — keep only the features that are essential to the core experience. What did you cut? Was it painful? What does that tell you about what your game is really about?

modules.title: Opening the Black Box
modules.overview: Modern game engines do an enormous amount of work invisibly — which can make it hard for designers to understand what is actually happening under the hood. This module demystifies the game engine by examining its core systems: the game loop, rendering pipeline, physics simulation, input handling, and audio engine. Understanding these systems helps designers make better-informed decisions, communicate more effectively with engineers, and anticipate the technical constraints that will shape their designs. No prior programming experience is required.
objectives: Describe the core systems of a game engine and how they interact to produce a running game
Explain the game loop and its implications for design decisions and performance
Identify how rendering, physics, and audio systems affect and constrain design choices
Use engine profiling and diagnostic tools to identify basic performance issues in a prototype

resources.label: Game Programming Patterns — Game Loop
Unity — Unity Profiler Walkthrough & Tutorial
Godot Engine — free/open-source engine with built-in Profiler

modules.reflectionPrompt: Think about a design idea you have had that you were not sure was technically feasible. After this module, do you have a better sense of whether it is possible — and what the trade-offs might be? What would you ask an engineer to help you understand better?

modules.title: Demonstrating Game Ideas
modules.overview: Before a game gets made, it must be communicated — to collaborators, publishers, investors, or players. This module focuses on the art and craft of demonstrating game ideas: how to create compelling pitches, design documents, vertical slices, and playable demos that convey the essence of a game to different audiences. You will practice presenting your game idea in multiple formats — verbal, written, and interactive — and receive structured feedback on the clarity, persuasiveness, and accuracy of your demonstrations.
objectives: Identify the appropriate format for demonstrating a game idea to different audiences (publishers, teammates, players)
Create a concise, compelling pitch for an original game concept in both verbal and written forms
Design or describe a vertical slice that demonstrates a game's core experience authentically
Give and receive structured, actionable feedback on game pitches and demonstrations
topics: Pitch Formats: Elevator Pitch, One-Pager, Full Pitch

resources.label: New Mexico State University Learning Games Lab Toolkit — Presentation Final Game Pitch
tinyBuildGAMES — How to Pitch Games (in 2024), presentation by Alex Nichiporchik
Twine — official open-source interactive-story tool

modules.reflectionPrompt: Write a 60-second elevator pitch for your capstone game concept. Read it aloud and time it. What did you have to cut to fit the time? What does that cutting process reveal about what is most essential in your game?

modules.title: Business of Games
modules.overview: Understanding the business side of games is essential for any designer who wants to see their work reach players. This module covers the economics of the games industry: revenue models, publishing deals, self-publishing, crowdfunding, marketing fundamentals, and the financial realities of both indie and studio development. You will analyze different business models and their player experience implications, examine the ethics of monetization, and develop a basic business plan for a hypothetical game project.
objectives: Describe the major revenue models used in the games industry: premium, free-to-play, subscription, and hybrid
Compare the trade-offs between self-publishing, traditional publishing, and crowdfunding
Identify the key components of a game marketing plan and community-building strategy
Develop a basic business plan for a hypothetical game project, including revenue model and target market
topics: Games Industry Overview and Market Size

resources.label: Newzoo's Global Games Market Report 2026 — Free Edition
Growing your mobile game — Unity Learn
Kickstarter Creator Handbook

modules.reflectionPrompt: Choose a revenue model for your capstone game concept and justify it. Why does that model fit your game's design and target audience? What are the ethical implications of that model — and how would you address them in your design?

modules.title: Industry Voices I
modules.overview: Hear directly from working professionals across the games industry — designers, producers, studio leads, and developers — about their careers, creative processes, and the lessons they have learned from shipped games. This first installment focuses on career paths into the industry, what it is like to work in a game studio, and how professionals approach the design challenges they face every day. Their perspectives will help you connect the skills you are building to the realities of professional practice.
objectives: Identify diverse career paths into and within the games industry across different roles and studio sizes
Describe the day-to-day realities of working as a game designer in a professional studio context
Reflect on how industry professionals approach design challenges, creative decisions, and collaboration
Connect industry perspectives to your own developing design practice and career goals

resources.label: ScreenSkills — Careers in games

Ubisoft — How to Prepare Yourself to be Employed as a Junior Games Designer (Zachary Preece)

modules.reflectionPrompt: After hearing from industry professionals, which career path resonates most with you — and why? What skills or experiences do you still need to develop? What is one concrete step you could take in the next month to move toward that path?

modules.title: Industry Voices II
modules.overview: This module continues the conversation with industry professionals, turning the spotlight on specialized disciplines and unconventional paths. You will hear from sound designers, narrative designers, accessibility advocates, and independent developers who have charted their own routes through the industry. Their perspectives illuminate the full spectrum of creative contributions that make games come alive, and offer insight into the emerging trends and opportunities shaping the future of the field.
objectives: Describe the craft and role of specialized game development disciplines including sound design and narrative design
Analyze how independent developers approach creative and business challenges differently from studio developers
Identify emerging trends and opportunities in the games industry based on practitioner perspectives
Articulate how the perspectives heard in this module inform your own approach to game design and career planning

Game Accessibility Guidelines — Full list

modules.reflectionPrompt: Which specialized discipline covered in this module — sound design, narrative design, accessibility, or independent development — most changed how you think about your own design practice? What is one thing you will do differently in your capstone project as a result?

modules.title: Designing a Game I
modules.overview: This is the first of two capstone modules in which you apply everything you have learned to design an original game from concept to functional prototype. In this module, you will define your game concept, write a design brief, build an initial prototype, and conduct a first round of structured playtesting. The emphasis is on moving quickly from idea to testable artifact — and using early feedback to sharpen your design direction before committing to a full iteration cycle in the next module.
objectives: Define and articulate an original game concept in a structured design brief
Build an initial prototype that embodies the core mechanic of your game concept
Conduct a structured playtest session and document observations and feedback systematically
Use playtest findings to identify the most critical design problems to address in the next iteration

modules.reflectionPrompt: After your first playtest of your capstone prototype, what is the single most important thing you learned about your game? Was it something you expected, or did it surprise you? How will it change the direction of your design in Module 24?

modules.title: Designing a Game II
modules.overview: In this final capstone module, you iterate on your game prototype based on playtest feedback, refine the design, and prepare a complete presentation of your work. You will add your completed game to your Game Diary as a professional portfolio piece, reflecting on what you designed, why you made the decisions you did, and what you would do differently. The module concludes with peer presentations — a celebration of the design journey and a demonstration of the full range of skills you have developed throughout the certificate.
objectives: Iterate on a game prototype based on structured playtest feedback from Module 23
Prepare a complete game presentation including concept, prototype, and design rationale
Document the full design process in your Game Diary as a professional portfolio piece
Reflect critically on your design decisions and articulate the lessons learned throughout the certificate
